To Infinity and Beyond 
Team ID#16287 
 
Sept. 19, 2023 -We learned about the surface of the moon, the moon's environment, and the 
simulated moon regolith. We walked out to the school sunflower garden and dug up a sunflower 
and found a very strong taproot. We learned new facts about sunflowers: can clean up toxic 
soil, have strong taproots, store pollution in leaves, love lots of sun, can live without a lot of 
water, and all parts of sunflowers are edible. When considering all these traits, we decided to 
plant sunflowers for our challenge. In our school garden, we have large sunflowers for our bees. 
We decided to plant dwarf sunflower seeds so they could grow in small pots. Our main reason 
for picking sunflowers was because they need lots of sun, and the moon receives 14 straight 
days of sun. Our teachers also told us there is some water on the moon. We know that 
sunflowers don’t need a lot of water, so that was another reason we decided to plant dwarf 
sunflower seeds. We talked about NASA going into space. We learned that NASA has to limit 
weight they can put on a rocket, so we cannot take a lot water or soil from the Earth to the 
Moon. We decided to mix different amounts of moon regolith with Earth soil (potting soil). 
Setting up TEAMS: Each student was assigned a job and a group to work with. Our 
photo/video team members planted the control pot, so they would not touch the moon regolith 
and transfer it to the iPad. Everyone on the team had an important job. 
Sept. 26, 2023: We mixed potting soil with moon regolith and planted dwarf sunflower seeds in 
pots. We also added distilled water. We put our plants in an outdoor plastic greenhouse. 
Descriptive Name: How do dwarf sunflowers grow in different mixtures of Earth soil and Moon 
regolith? 
Hypothesis: Can a dwarf sunflower taproot break through 
moon regolith? 
Independent Variable: Soil composition 
Dependent Variable: Length of taproot 
Measurements: We used rulers to measure the height in 
centimeters. Also, we counted the number of leaves on 
each plant. We measured once a week (Tuesdays) and 
kept track of the weather. We gave each plant 100mL of 
distilled water every week. We learned how to measure 
with a graduated cylinder. We also looked for taproots to 
measure at the end of the planting period. 
Control: Dwarf Sunflower seed grown in 100% potting soil. 
Constants: All plants (control and experimental) were 
housed in a greenhouse outside. All plants received 
100mL of distilled water weekly and were in the same environment and temperature.

Describe what happened? 
● Our class meets once a week on Tuesdays. During our class time, we watered our 
plants with 100mL of distilled water, measured their height in centimeters, and counted 
the number of leaves growing on each plant. Plants were housed in our greenhouse. 
● During our Fall Break, our teacher watered and measured our plants for us. 
● We met on Oct. 17th. We had 
three plants growing at that time, 
so we decided not to replant. Our 
Control Pot was 1.6 cm (still a 
sprout). Pot 7 was 4.5 cm with 10 
leaves, and Pot 8 was 7.5 cm with 
8 leaves. 
 
 
WEEK 8 
Results: 
Pot #7 5.6 cm and 10 leaves 
Pot #8 16.4 cm and 16 leaves 
 
The official challenge ended week 8. However, 
we did not have time to unpot and check for 
taproots until week 9. Below are our results 
from Week 9. 
The plant in our Control Pot ended up dying, but Pot #7 & Pot #8 kept 
growing. We didn’t get any growth in any of our other pots. Pot #7 
Pot #8 both had 75% regolith and 25 % potting soil. Pot #9 also had 
75% regolith and 25% potting soil, but it did not grow. 
 
 
 
 
By the end of 9 weeks, we had two pots with 
growth. Pot #7 was 8 cm tall with 10 leaves, and 
Pot #8 was 23 cm tall with 23 leaves.

We thought we found some taproots, but we decided later that they were not taproots. We 
thought the longest root might be a taproot, but it wasn’t either. We did research on Dwarf 
Sunflowers and learned that they take a long time to grow a taproot and need very moist soil. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* We only measured at the beginning, midpoint, 8 weeks and then again at 9 weeks when 
we had time to open the pots and look for taproots.

What Would We Do Differently? 
● Add fertilizer. 
● Have more control pots. 
● Water at least 2x a week, so the soil stays moist and can grow a taproot. 
● Try different amounts of regolith and potting soil. 
● Move the greenhouse inside and add a heat lamp on a timer to expose sunflowers to 
more heat and light. 
What Did We Learn? 
● Never give up. 
● Sunflowers need more sun, heat, and water. 
● In our school garden and pulled up sunflowers to see what a large taproot looks like. 
● Sunflower roots can grow in regolith. 
● How to measure with a ruler using centimeters and a graduated cylinder. 
● How to set-up a graph. 
● We learned that NASA can’t take loads of soil and water to the moon, so we are trying to 
help them find a way to grow plants on the moon. 
Coolest Thing We Discovered 
● The 75% regolith/25% potting soil felt and looked like kinetic sand. 
● Roots can grow through regolith, so it could be possible to plant the moon. 
What Would You Tell Others About Your Experiment? 
● Give your plants a lot of sun and keep the soil moist.
